data.title: GrubMarket launches AI Agent to turn invoices into purchase orders
data.description:
GrubMarket, a South San Francisco, California-based software-as-a-service (SAAS) company working with food producers, wholesalers, distributors and retailers, is expanding its use of artificial intelligence (AI) with a new AI agent. The company designed its new AI agent to turn vendor invoices and receipts into purchase orders for food distributors. The tool, called the “AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent,” was made to reduce the amount of manual data entry required from produce and other fresh food distributors.

“The food supply chain industry is undergoing unprecedented transformation driven by artificial intelligence,” said Mike Xu, CEO of GrubMarket, in a release statement. “With our new AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent, we are bringing powerful AI capabilities to another critical function within food distribution.”

The new agent follows other recent AI rollouts from GrubMarket. In June, the company announced the launch of an AI sales agent. Its other AI deployments have included a reporting AI agent on its GrubAssist AI platform. GrubMarket also created its Monitoring AI Agent that tracks financial and operational data for customers.

Now, the technology provider is turning to purchase orders.

Why GrubMarket launched its new AI agent

Xu said that by automating purchasing workflows, GrubMarket is helping distributors operate more efficiently. In turn, he believes that they can gain better visibility into their businesses, making better-informed decisions and improving profitability.

“This launch represents another important step in our broader vision of building specialized AI agents that automate and optimize every major function across the food supply chain industry,” Xu said, adding that the company remains committed to leveraging artificial intelligence to help businesses modernize their operations and unlock new levels of efficiency and growth.

Industry observers said the real test will be in the details.

Amy Dean, vice president of operations at SC Codeworks, a Columbus, Ohio-based warehouse management software company, said that every company handles purchase order entry differently. However, she sees it is most likely being driven by spreadsheets, ERP systems and planners.

“AI has the potential to reduce repetitive data entry, which would free up employees to handle exceptions, vendor relationships, and more strategic purchasing activities,” Dean said.

She noted AI will need to navigate special challenges that come with the food business.

“Food distribution especially is not always straightforward,” she assessed. “There are many variables that change often, such as recalls, substitutions, and vendor-specific requirements.”

Dean, who is an operations and IT expert with over a decade of experience in logistics, believes that it will be “critical that all of that is accounted for in the logic that is used with an AI agent.”

Moreover, she sees access to accurate data as a vital part of the new agent’s success.

“The ability for an AI agent to read invoices, receipts and photos could be beneficial for organizations that don’t currently utilize integration tools,” Dean stated. “However, that AI agent is only as effective as the data it has access to. This is where inventory accuracy becomes critical and current business processes can make or break the success.”

Larger challenges for the new agent

Dmytro Klymentiev is an AI systems engineer in Chicago who builds AI automation and ERP systems for businesses. He said reading a photo of an invoice and pulling out the line items is no longer the hard part. In his view, that is because most current AI models can do it. What GrubMarket adds, he said, is the connection. The extracted data becomes a structured purchase order inside the distributor’s own system, matched to its catalog.

“That is useful, but I would call it an incremental step rather than a new way of purchasing,” Klymentiev said.

In his view, the time savings are narrower than they look. He pointed out that while nobody needs to type out an order, someone may still need to check each draft to avoid knock-on effects from errors.

“A misread quantity or a wrong product match turns into a wrong order, then a wrong delivery, a failed invoice match and wrong stock levels,” Klymentiev stated. “The work moves from data entry to review, and the review has to be careful.”

Before adopting a tool like this, he recommends that distributors ask whether it flags a line or guesses when it’s unsure, how it matches products to their catalog, what happens with new or renamed items, and whether they can measure its error rate on their own documents before it touches live orders.

data.title: Under Armour Q2 sales slide as CEO cites optimism about AI
data.description:
Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank spoke in optimistic terms about the sports apparel and equipment brand’s road ahead, even as net revenue fell 6.9% year over year to $1.24 billion in the fiscal second quarter ended Sept. 30.

“We delivered against our revenue expectation and exceeded our operating income outlook,” said Plank in the company’s earnings announcement. “As we progress in this transformation, we are driving greater efficiency across our business, sharpening our product offering, and amplifying global marketing to strengthen our brand and improve financial performance.”

In the meantime, Under Armour shared that it incurred a total of $13 million in Q2 costs released to its Fiscal 2025 Restructuring Plan, which expects to be “substantially complete” by the end of 2026. It expects full fiscal year revenue to ultimately fall year over year “at a mid-single-digit percentage rate.”

Under Armour is No. 158 in the Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Under Armour wholesale and ecommerce sales in Q2

“Wholesale revenue decreased 6% to $725 million, reflecting the impact of softer full-price sell-through and pressure in parts of the distributor business, partly offset by select accounts and markets,” Plank told investors on Under Armour’s Q2 earnings call. “Direct-to-consumer revenue decreased 8% to $494 million, including a 7% decline in owned and operated stores and a 12% decline in ecommerce.”

Plank attributed the drops to a reduction in overall traffic.

“Traffic remained the primary challenge, particularly in North America, with better conversion and targeted digital initiatives providing some offset,” he stated.

How Plank expects Under Armour to benefit from AI

Speaking to analysts on the Nov. 6 earnings call, Plank touched on the role he sees artificial intelligence (AI) playing as Under Armour seeks to complete a turnaround for its business.

“I think that our industry actually lines and maps up perfectly for the advantage of what AI brings for us,” he stated.

Primarily, he noted that he believes the company needs to focus on three areas to realize benefits from AI. Those include supply chain, merchandising and marketing.

Nevertheless, he cautioned that the answer to solving Under Armour’s problems would have to eventually address one topic: “ship us everything that we ordered.” In that context, he added that “accuracy and delivering on time and full is also a priority.”

data.title: Asics uses AI-powered drones to recover misplaced inventory 60% faster
data.description:
Asics America Corp. is using autonomous drones to find misplaced merchandise at its primary North American distribution center, a move the company says is helping it curb the risk of unfulfilled orders.

The technology, developed by Corvus Robotics, is helping the sportswear brand recover misplaced inventory about 60% faster, according to a Nov. 10 announcement from the warehouse automation provider.

At Asics’ facility in Byhalia, Mississippi, drones now conduct inventory counts in two key storage areas every month, up from twice annually. The higher frequency lets Asics offer merchandise on online marketplaces that were previously withheld due to fulfillment concerns.

Asics America, based in Irvine, California, is the U.S. subsidiary of Japanese sportswear company Asics Corp.

How Asics uses drones to count warehouse inventory

Asics’ 855,000-square-foot distribution center in Byhalia houses nearly 3 million units of footwear, apparel and accessories across roughly 44,000 stock-keeping units.

The facility fulfills ecommerce orders while also supplying Asics stores and wholesale customers. All three channels draw from the same inventory pool, and customer returns are processed there as well.

Asics is using Corvus One drones in two warehouse zones: a singles area that stores returned merchandise and individual pairs of shoes, and a case reserve area that holds full cartons.

The drones perform seven scheduled flights a night, starting at around 7 p.m., Corvus said. Using onboard computer vision and spatial reasoning, they navigate aisles less than 6 feet wide without needing additional warehouse infrastructure, such as markers or beacons.

During each flight, the drones scan universal product codes while also counting boxes stored at each location. Corvus said the system compares those counts with barcode scans, identifying inventory discrepancies. The following morning, a warehouse employee reviews the results using images and video captured during the flights.

“Now we can just look at the footage and we can tell exactly what’s going on with it in the locations before we have to send someone out,” Angela Williford, inventory control operations manager at Asics America, said in a Corvus video case study. “If it’s something that we can correct from the desk, we’ll correct it then.”

More frequent counts help Asics recover merchandise

During one three-month period, drones identified 26 misplaced cases containing more than 200 pairs of shoes. Without the additional counts, those items could have remained unavailable for sale until the next scheduled inventory review, Asics said.

Koestler estimated that Asics is recovering misplaced inventory roughly 60% faster than before the deployment.

“You don’t want to have to count a thousand locations to find the four or five that have problems,” he said in the video case study.

The automation has also shifted how warehouse employees spend their time. Rather than focusing on routine cycle counts, workers can dedicate more effort to inventory reconciliation, discrepancy investigations and wholesale-support projects, according to the companies.

Corvus also said the drones reduce the need for lift equipment during inventory counts, limiting traffic in the facility’s narrow aisles.

Asics makes more inventory available to marketplaces

The inventory gains have also influenced how Asics sells products through online marketplaces.

Before adopting the drone system, Asics withheld between 12 and 15 units out of every 100 from the inventory feeds it provided to marketplace partners, according to Corvus. The company did so because products shown as available might be missing or difficult to locate when orders arrived.

With monthly counts providing greater visibility into stock levels, Asics said it now publishes its full inventory availability feed.

Corvus said the change allows Asics to offer more merchandise at full price rather than potentially liquidating it at a discount. The companies did not disclose how much additional revenue the change has generated.

Other retailers expand warehouse automation

Asics is among a growing number of companies deploying inventory drones to improve warehouse operations.

After deploying Corvus’ technology, health and wellness retailer GNC increased inventory counts at its distribution centers in Indianapolis and Phoenix, according to a case study. Counts rose to as many as 10 to 12 times per year, up from two to four.

Likewise, Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits expanded its drone deployment to nine distribution centers. The beverage distributor reported a 100-basis-point improvement in cases handled per hour, Corvus said.

Other major retailers are investing in different forms of warehouse automation. Walmart Inc. recently announced plans to expand Symbotic automation technology across 25 U.S. regional distribution centers. The retailer said the rollout is designed to support inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve product flow throughout its supply chain.

Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

data.title: Lowe's partners with Bilt to expand loyalty rewards, AI-powered commerce
data.description:
Lowe’s Companies Inc. has partnered with housing rewards platform Bilt to expand its loyalty reach. The partnership lets Bilt members earn points on Lowe’s purchases and use those rewards toward a home maintenance subscription.

Announced Nov. 10, the tie-up makes Lowe’s Bilt’s exclusive home improvement partner, connecting the retailer with the platform’s more than 8 million members. The companies also plan to launch a curated Lowe’s marketplace within Bilt in early 2027.

“By partnering with Bilt, we can meet customers in a community they already know and love and connect them to Lowe’s products, services and rewards in a way that feels simple and seamless,” said Jen Wilson, Lowe’s executive vice president and chief marketing officer, in the company’s announcement.

The partnership runs on Bilt’s new Neighborhood OS. The artificial intelligence (AI)-powered commerce platform helps businesses reach nearby consumers with personalized offers and loyalty benefits.

Lowe’s ranks No. 9 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Lowe’s is No. 90 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

How Lowe’s and Bilt rewards work together

Bilt members can now earn rewards through both loyalty programs.

Its members can link an existing MyLowe’s Rewards account — or create one — to earn one Bilt Point per dollar on eligible Lowe’s purchases. Additionally, they can earn MyLowe’s Money through the retailer’s loyalty program. MyLowe’s Rewards benefits include free shipping and exclusive member deals.

The agreement adds Lowe’s to Bilt’s network of more than 50,000 merchant partners nationwide, including restaurants and fitness studios. Through Neighborhood OS, Lowe’s can reach members with offers and rewards based on where they live and direct them to nearby stores.

The partnership also gives members another way to pay for Lowe’s home maintenance services. Bilt members can use Bilt Points, Bilt Cash or a linked payment card to purchase a Lowe’s HomeCare+ subscription, the companies said.

The subscription costs $99 annually and includes two in-home visits by trained Lowe’s associates, covering up to seven maintenance services. Subscribers also receive 5% off products used during those services and Gold MyLowe’s Rewards benefits. HomeCare+ is available in select ZIP codes and renews each year automatically.

Bilt’s Neighborhood OS manages enrollment, checks service availability at members’ addresses and processes subscription payments, Lowe’s said. The companies plan to add matching with existing MyLowe’s Rewards accounts in December.

How Bilt Neighborhood OS uses AI to connect businesses and shoppers

Bilt’s Neighborhood OS connects with businesses’ existing payment, reservation and customer-management systems. This allows merchants to target nearby shoppers with offers, recognize returning customers and track spending tied to promotions.

“For example, a neighborhood restaurant can identify prospective customers, launch a targeted offer to bring them in, recognize them when they visit, and automatically apply the appropriate benefit through its existing point-of-sale system,” Bilt said in its announcement.

The platform also uses AI agents to manage tasks such as reservations, customer communications and marketing across those connected systems.

In the 30 days before its announcement, Bilt said its AI agents completed more than 2 million actions across more than 29,000 businesses, with 91% of those actions requiring no human intervention.

The platform builds on Bilt’s expansion beyond rent rewards. Founded in 2021, the company has added mortgage rewards, local shopping, travel and home services.

Bilt estimates that roughly $6.6 trillion in annual U.S. retail and food-services spending takes place in person. Its members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local businesses over the past 12 months, the company said.

How loyalty rewards influence shopping behavior

Lowe’s brings an established loyalty program to the partnership. MyLowe’s Rewards had more than 30 million members, who shopped twice as often and spent more than 50% more than nonmembers, the retailer said in its 2025 annual report.

Bilt’s research points to consumers’ willingness to try nearby businesses that offer rewards. In its first-ever State of the Neighborhood 2026 study, 95% of respondents said they would try a local business at least once if they could earn points or rewards there. Another 87% said they would shop more frequently at a local business offering those incentives.

The study also found that two-thirds of Americans make at least 80% of their everyday spending within their neighborhoods, with the median consumer shopping within 15 miles of home. Conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global on Bilt’s behalf, the survey covered 6,591 U.S. adults in March and April 2026.

Bilt expands partnerships across retail, technology and services
